canonical_topic: Gas Pressure, Volume, and Temperature Interdependence (Ideal Gas Law)
definition: Unlike solids or liquids, a gas's volume changes readily with outside conditions, and its pressure, volume, and temperature are mutually interdependent — none can change without affecting the others. The ideal gas law gives an approximate, layman-level description of this relationship for gases whose molecular collisions are treated as perfectly elastic.
core_idea: Gas moves from high-pressure to low-pressure areas until pressure equalizes (the mechanism behind both straws and pipelines), and compressing a gas raises its temperature while letting it expand lowers its temperature. The ideal gas law formalizes how pressure, volume, and temperature move together, e.g., at constant volume, a temperature rise forces a pressure rise.
key_points: Gas expands to fill its container unless constrained, and flows from high-pressure to low-pressure regions until equalized; a larger pressure differential moves gas faster.
Compressing a gas raises its temperature; letting it disperse or expand lowers its temperature.
Cooling a gas below the boiling point of any trace component can cause that component to condense into liquid — relevant since fuel gases like methane are rarely pure and carry trace gases.
Holding volume constant, raising a gas's temperature forces its pressure to rise, and vice versa, since the ideal gas law is an equality.
The ideal gas law is presented as a reasonable, layman-level approximation, not an exact model — it assumes perfectly elastic molecular collisions.

General relationships noted: gas in a contained area gets hotter as its pressure increases (and cooler as pressure decreases); cooling a gas lets more of it fit in the same volume at constant pressure.
relationships: Explains why pipeline compressors change both pressure and temperature simultaneously
Explains liquid dropout risk in pipelines and gas processing
trading_implications: Trace-gas condensation risk ties gas composition/quality to pipeline operability, relevant to quality specifications embedded in physical gas transport contracts.
caveats: Pressure, volume, and temperature cannot be treated independently — changing one always affects the others under the ideal gas law.
